title: Climate variability and dysentery morbidity in Gambella Region, Ethiopia: A retrospective ecological time-series analysis, 2012–2021
content:
by Geteneh Moges Assefa

Background

Evidence on meteorological variability and dysentery morbidity in Ethiopia remains limited. We examined associations between monthly temperature, rainfall, relative humidity and surveillance-reported dysentery in three Gambella woredas.

Methods

A separate 1992–2021 meteorological series provided descriptive climatic context. This retrospective ecological time-series study linked monthly surveillance and meteorological data from September 2012 to December 2021. Negative binomial candidate models evaluated exposures at lags of 0–2 months using a common dataset of 330 woreda-month observations. Models included a population offset, woreda fixed effects, month-of-year indicators and a smooth temporal trend. The selected model used natural cubic splines for same-month exposures. We estimated exposure–response curves with 95% confidence intervals and assessed residual autocorrelation, an autoregressive sensitivity model and exclusion of 2020–2021.

Results

The full surveillance dataset contained 6,723 cases; the regression sample contained 6,587. The same-month spline model had the lowest Akaike Information Criterion among candidate models. Overall associations were detected for temperature (χ2 = 13.77, p = 0.003), rainfall (χ2 = 44.15, p < 0.001) and humidity (χ2 = 28.43, p < 0.001). Relative incidence at the 90th exposure percentile versus the median was 1.23 (95% CI 1.03–1.47) for temperature and 1.17 (1.06–1.29) for humidity. Rainfall showed a steep increase from very dry to moderate conditions and a comparatively flat middle-to-upper range. Overall associations persisted in sensitivity analyses, although evidence for temperature was weaker before 2020.

Conclusions

Short-term meteorological variability was associated with reported dysentery morbidity. These ecological associations support further investigation of locally calibrated surveillance integrating meteorological, flooding, water, sanitation and reporting information. They do not establish causal effects or validated outbreak-prediction thresholds.
